rows.description: The toddler shakes her head, throws food or says no: a first taste of choice and control, not defiance. Offer small healthy choices, keep meals calm, and do not fight over each bite.
Forced feeding, threats or chasing with a plate make food a battle and can create fear at the table. Parents should offer, model eating together, and trust hunger to do its work.
Eating in a lap or with family, sharing roti or rice, feels like being loved. Toddler smiles and copies. Regular shared meals build belonging; avoid screens at the table.
I fear a friend is in real danger, such as self-neglect or unsafe home. Wise: breaking a secret to a trusted adult can be love, and tell the friend I am doing so. Harmful: carrying it alone.

A friend confides something painful. I feel honoured and scared. Wise: listen, do not joke, keep it private, and encourage them to tell a trusted adult. Harmful: promising total secrecy when they may be in danger.

A younger friend tells me I am their hero and shares everything. I feel proud and pressured. Wise: stay honest about my flaws and point them to other supports. Harmful: leaning into control because they listen.
A friend leans on me at all hours and I am worn out. Wise: care, set limits, and encourage other support like family or a counsellor. Harmful: quietly resenting them.
Feels betrayed and wants to expose them back; cooling down, confronting privately and deciding whether trust can be rebuilt is a better path.
I leaked a friend's secret out of excitement and now I cannot face them. Wise: apologise plainly with no excuse, accept their anger, and give distance. Harmful: denying it or blaming them.
They deny leaking and say I am overreacting or imagining it. Wise: trust my own memory, keep details, and step back. This is not my fault. Harmful: doubting myself until I apologise.
Chooses to forgive after a sincere apology while adjusting how much to share; forgiveness is not forgetting.
A feverish or hurt child wants to be held and will not be put down. Comfort, water, rest and a steady voice are right; call a doctor for high fever or worrying signs, and never scold clinginess.

White coats, injections and strange rooms frighten a toddler, who cries and resists. Parents stay close, hold the child, tell the truth simply (a small pinch), and never threaten the doctor as punishment.
A kiss on the scrape and a hug after a fall tell the child her pain matters. Acknowledging the hurt first and calmly, without saying it is nothing, teaches trust and later resilience.

I am compared aloud at family gatherings and feel judged in front of everyone. It is not my fault, and their pride and anxiety are the source. Wise: ask privately to stop and show effort on my own terms.

I resent my parent and quietly dislike the cousin who did nothing wrong. Wise: tell the parent how comparison lands and ask for support with my own targets. Immature: sabotaging my work to prove them wrong.

I stop reacting to comparisons and go numb, telling myself I do not care. Wise: check whether I truly stopped caring or just stopped feeling; then have one honest talk. Harmful: turning off effort altogether.

As a parent I compare my child because I fear they will fall behind and I feel my own regrets. Wise: notice that comparison motivates rarely, and praise real effort. Harmful: making love feel conditional.

Kids say "you can't play with us". I feel a stone in my tummy and tears come. It is not because I am bad. Wise action: tell a teacher or find another game. A grown-up can help by making a place for me.
The teacher sees me alone and sits beside me, then invites others to join. I feel seen and less lonely. Wise adults help without embarrassing the child and without forcing others to like them.
A child calls "come, you can be the goalkeeper!" I feel warm relief, as if I belong. I remember who invited me and try to invite others. Being welcomed teaches me to welcome the next child.
Nobody notices me on the playground and I stand alone. I feel invisible. A wise adult helps me practise a friendly line or plans a small play date. Loneliness at this age needs adult help, not shame.
